prompt.context: A friend of mine at MIT has come to us for help. He was given a $20 million grant to think of a cool, yet socially responsible, technology. After some time, he has finally created a product that is on the brink of commercialization. It's a GPS device that is placed into a car and senses the type and severity of a car accident. It immediately transmits this information back to emergency services, which then deploys resources to the accident scene. This service is most valuable for the more severe accidents, otherwise known as 'Type A' accidents. At this point, my friend is considering a pilot in the Chicago area.
prompt.question: Before he moves forward, he would like us to help him answer two questions: (1) How large is this market opportunity? (2) What methods should he use to price the device?

clarifying_info.q: How many cars are in the Chicago area?
What percentage of cars get into Type A accidents per year?
clarifying_info.a: 1% of cars get into Type A accidents per year

clarifying_info.q: What is the average Type A accident medical claim?
clarifying_info.a: The average Type A accident medical claim is $100,000

clarifying_info.q: How much does the new device save per claim?
clarifying_info.a: The new device should save $50,000 per claim

Market opportunity = the size of the potential market if the product reached 100% market saturation and extracted 100% of the value of the product. Focus on medical claims only and the Chicago market.

clarifying_info.q: What does the device cost to make?
clarifying_info.a: Fully-loaded device costs $400 (this is cost of making the device, not the sale price)

framework: Size the market opportunity for Chicago by estimating Type A accidents per year and the value saved per accident (medical claims focus)
Identify all stakeholders who benefit from the device to inform pricing strategy
Analyze pricing methods: cost-plus, value-based, competitor-based, and others
Consider environmental factors: patent defensibility, government mandates, OEM/mechanic distribution channels
Set pricing objective (profit maximization, revenue maximization, quality leadership, survival, etc.)

questions.prompt: Question 1: How large is the market opportunity in Chicago?
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure as: Market Opportunity = Device Savings Per Claim x Type A Accidents Per Year. A good answer reaches $500M. A better answer uses a clear structured framework. A superior answer also discusses new product diffusion curves, other value drivers beyond claims savings, and device compatibility across car types. Candidate should focus on Type A accidents and medical claims only; avoid getting stuck debating the definition of market opportunity.

math.setup: Market Opportunity = Device Savings Per Claim x Type A Accidents Per Year
steps: Type A Accidents Per Year = 1,000,000 cars x 1% = 10,000 accidents

questions.prompt: Question 2: What methods should be used to price this device? (qualitative)
questions.guidance: A good answer covers the pricing strategy framework: (1) marketing analysis — customer segments, targeting, positioning, and competitors/substitutes; (2) marketing mix decisions; (3) demand curve estimation; (4) cost calculation; (5) environmental factors; (6) pricing objective selection; (7) pricing methods. A better/superior answer identifies multiple customers (end user AND insurance companies), discusses environmental factors such as patent defensibility and potential government mandates, and probes the implications of key stakeholders (government mandating device, OEMs/mechanics installing it, investors needing return, community social mandates, competitors imitating).

brainstorming.prompt: Who are the stakeholders interested in or affected by this GPS device, and what is their stake?

categories.name: End users
ideas: Car drivers who benefit from faster emergency response
Community members benefiting from reduced accident severity

categories.name: Commercial entities
ideas: Insurance companies (health, life, P&C) saving on claims
OEMs (e.g., Ford) that could install device in new cars
Mechanics installing devices in used cars
Investors seeking financial return on the $20M grant technology

categories.name: Government & public sector
ideas: Government — could mandate the device, driving mass adoption
Emergency services receiving faster, more accurate accident data
Medical community benefiting from faster response times

categories.name: Competitive landscape
ideas: Competitors who may imitate the device (patent defensibility question)

recommendation: The Chicago market opportunity based on medical claims savings for Type A accidents is approximately $500 million annually

Pricing should be value-based given the significant $50,000 savings per claim, targeting insurance companies as primary customers alongside end users, and leveraging potential government mandates to drive adoption
risks: Patent may not be defensible, inviting rapid imitation and price compression
Adoption curve may be slow without a mandate; 100% market saturation assumption may overstate near-term opportunity
Device cost of $400 constrains pricing floor and margin
next_steps: Conduct patent analysis to assess defensibility
Engage insurance companies to quantify willingness to pay and subsidy potential
Evaluate government lobbying strategy to accelerate mandate consideration
Design pilot pricing structure for Chicago market test
